center_of_gravity: The physical shift in where quantity and custody reside in clay: from three-dimensional counters enclosed within hollow clay envelopes to impressions visible directly on the surface of solid tablets.
what_is_happening: A spoken-word reconstruction of ordinary Late Uruk clay practices: handling loose geometric counters, enclosing them inside hollow clay balls with rolled seals and exterior impressions, and impressing numerical marks with reeds directly onto solid clay tablets.
what_changes_during_passage: The physical condition of inspecting quantity and authentication: moving from hidden contents requiring destruction of the envelope to marks inspectable directly on a durable clay surface, while both practices continue to coexist.
begins_at: Handling loose geometric clay counters between fingers in Late Uruk administrative contexts.
stops_before: The emergence of proto-cuneiform pictographic tablets with ruled compartments and complex commodity signs.
notebook_threads_to_use: Small geometric clay counters (spheres, cones, disks, cylinders) handling quantity in Late Uruk.
Hollow clay envelopes enclosing counters, creating a physical condition where inspection requires breaking.
Cylinder seals rolled across wet clay marking custody, authority, or witnessing.
Exterior impressions on envelopes mirroring enclosed quantities without immediate breakage.
Solid numerical tablets with reed impressions and seal rollings.
Coexistence and overlapping of these media without an evolutionary ladder or direct replacement.
deliberately_unused_threads: Proto-cuneiform pictographic tablets with ruled compartments and commodity/institutional signs (Uruk IV).
Clay sealings on cord, cloth, or wooden door closures.
Specific museum specimen numbers (OIM A64678, ChM III-937a) and site-specific provenance details.
